messages.subject: hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
Hi,

I'm working on a random slopes and intercepts logistic regression, and I'd greatly appreciate feedback on whether or not I've implemented this in Stan correctly. I've attached my Stan code. The current model has 1 factor with 4 levels and 1 (continuous) predictor variable. I'd like to expand the analysis to include more factors and continuous predictors. Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
Jeanne

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
Looks OK, but what you want to do to test is simulate data from the model
and make sure you can recover the parameters.

I'd also recommend vectorizing this:

for(i in 1:N){
mu = beta[1] + c_c[1, cer_class[i]] + (beta[2] + c_c[2, cer_class[i]]) * x1[i];
y[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu);
}

to

mu = beta[1] + cc[1, cer_class] + (beta[2] + cc[2, cer_class]) .* x1;
y ~ bernoulli_logit(mu);

You'll need to declare x1 a row_vector for this to work because cc[2, cer_class]
is a row vector (defined by cc[2, cer_class][i] = cc[2, cer_class[i]].

You can skip the mu if you don't want to save it and just write

y ~ bernoulli_logit(beta[1] + cc[1, cer_class]
+ (beta[2] + cc[2, cer_class]) .* x1);

I'd probably have defined two variables for the beta and two variables for
the cc in this small example, but the way you have it will generalize better.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
I think in your data block you should probably define x1 like:

row_vector<lower=0>[N] x1;

In the first file x1 was just an array of N reals, but changing it to this makes it a row_vector of N reals (that can be used as Bob suggested).

Ben

parts: You just need to generalize this
(beta[2] + cc[2, cer_class]) .* x

in which beta[2] and cc[2, cer_class[n]] and x[n] are
all scalars into one where they're all vectors. Then the
elementwise dot product will become a matrix multiply.

- Bob
